newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - Govt won't alter UK economy forecasts.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Govt won't alter UK economy forecasts.

text.p: Official British growth and inflation forecasts are expected to remain unchanged in the July 2 budget, a Reuters survey of economists' expectations showed.

In the survey, carried out between June 19 and 20, the median of 20 predictions showed Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown would give an official forecast for gross domestic product (GDP) of 3.5 percent for 1997 and retail prices excluding mortgage interest payments (RPIX) of 2.5 percent by quarter four 1997.
These would be unchanged from predictions made by the previous, Conservative, Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke in his budget last November.

"They will not assume the Bank of England is going to miss the inflation target and 3.5 percent GDP growth looks about right given the strength of consumer spending," said Andy Cates, UK economist at UBS.
Analysts say sterling, currently trading around 2.8800 marks, its highest level against the German currency for nearly five years, will keep a lid on inflation to end-1997.
On June 6, the Bank of England monetary policy committee made a pre-emptive strike against inflation by raising official interest rates to 6.5 percent from 6.25 percent.
Some analysts are expecting another 25 basis point rise to 6.75 percent at the council meeting on July 10.

Top of the poll's range of expectations for the official 1997 GDP forecast was one of 3.75 percent. The lowest prediction, three percent, came from the Centre for Economic and Business Research (CEBR), still well above estimated trend growth of 2.25 to 2.5 percent.
"We think there are some indications of a slight slowing, these will be reflected in official forecasts," said Mihir Warty, economist at the CEBR.
But the booming economy in 1997 is not expected to bring Britain's current account deficit with the world into balance.

The median of 19 analysts' expectations shows the government forecasting a shortfall of three billion sterling in 1997. Expectations ranged from no deficit at all to a current account deficit of six billion sterling.
The Conservative government in the last UK budget forecast a 4.25 billion sterling deficit for the current account in 1997.

Economists' predictions for official GDP forecasts in 1998 reflect expectations of a slowdown in the economy as higher interest rates start to bite. The median of 18 contributions to the survey show the government forecasting GDP at 2.7 percent.

Forecasts of a slower pace of growth were also reflected in a deteriorating outlook for the current account. The median of 14 contributions foresaw an official current account estimate for a deficit of 5.5 billion sterling in 1998.
